summary: A fiction excerpt (Book 15, part 175) in which Commander Ray and his crew confront a horrific scene of compressed, slaughtered bodies behind a door in a reactor control room. Ray recalls his childhood memory of making monkey bread, a sticky cinnamon-sugar biscuit dish, as he sees the grotesque mass of bodies that blots out the lights. Kilgore reports a new problem, and the crew retreats to a monitoring pod where systems still show green.
one_line: Commander Ray confronts a grisly chamber of packed bodies in a reactor control room, recalling childhood monkey bread while Kilgore reports a new problem.
key_facts: The note is titled "Book 15 — part 175" and is categorized under the source "books" in the fiction domain.
Ray cannot see how the bodies could fit the space, and the numbers 'just don't work' until Rodriguez leaves the door ajar and he goes to look.
Ray's memory of monkey bread dates to when he was a boy of eight or ten, when his mother discovered the recipe.
Monkey bread was made from canned biscuits twisted into shapes and packed tightly into a bundt cake pan, then soaked in a brown sugar syrup.
The monkey bread recipe was seasoned with cinnamon and sugar and lathered in butter and a corn syrup, brown sugar paste.
His mother liked monkey bread because it took all of twenty minutes from biscuit can to cooling on the counter.
The crew is packed so tightly that blood dribbles down the wall of packed flesh into a small and spreading pool at Ray's feet.
Ray can only see because of light through the open door, as the bodies have blotted out the ceiling lamps and desk equipment.
Ray says "You don't want to go in there" and closes the door.
Kilgore says to Ray: "Commander, I think you should have a look at this. We have a new problem."
Kilgore and Rodriguez have retreated to a wide, semi-circular panel display in the control room where the lights remain green.
The panel is a security and monitoring pod that does not have business with the reactor itself, which is why its lights stay green.
Ray sweats from the impossible heat generated by so much compressed mass.
